global.headline: TRUMP HALTS IRAN STRIKES FOR FIRST TIME IN TWO WEEKS AS HORMUZ TALKS ADVANCE; PENTAGON CASUALTY COUNT CONTROVERSY ERUPTS
summary: The US military carried out no strikes on Iran overnight Friday into Saturday — the first pause after 13 consecutive nights of CENTCOM attacks — as Oman-mediated talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz made what sources called positive, though still incomplete, progress. Trump said the war was "going extremely well" and that the US has "hit Iran very hard," but stopped short of confirming any ceasefire, saying strikes could resume or even "make it a heavier dose" if talks fail. Iran continues to insist all Hormuz traffic needs its approval and has attacked ships straying from its approved coastal route; Washington and its Gulf partners reject any Iranian right to impose routes, restrictions or tolls. Hormuz traffic stayed near a standstill regardless — just 6 commercial vessels transited on Thursday.

The pause did not extend to a second front: Iran-aligned Houthi rebels fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at two Saudi Aramco sites on the Red Sea coast, Jizan and Yanbu, on Saturday — the first direct strike on a Saudi refinery complex in four years — after Saudi-led forces struck Houthi positions in Hodeidah and Kamaran Island a day earlier. A Patriot battery operated by Greek forces intercepted two missiles aimed at Yanbu, which alone handled 92% of Saudi seaborne crude exports in June. Brent crude spiked briefly above $100/barrel on the news before easing back into the high-$80s/low-$90s range.

Separately, a Pentagon website tracking Iran-war casualties showed sharply reduced totals this week in what defence officials called a "data disruption": the confirmed US death toll fell from 18 to 14 — effectively removing the four service members killed in Jordan and Iraq since fighting resumed in late June — while the wounded count dropped from 482 to 420. The site remained uncorrected roughly a day later. Senate Democrats wrote to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding a full accounting, and New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she was "outraged" that Sgt Angel Rampersad, a New York native killed in the fighting, had been "removed" from the database. Separately, US intelligence assessed that Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei — unlike his father, who issued a fatwa against nuclear weapons — is significantly more willing to pursue them, focused less on a Hiroshima-yield device than on miniaturised thermonuclear warheads deliverable by long-range missile, the New York Times reported; officials cautioned there is no clear evidence Iran has restarted weapons-development work and much of the intelligence predates the war.
global.geopolitical: The first strike-free night in two weeks, alongside apparent progress in Oman-mediated Hormuz talks, is the clearest sign yet of a possible off-ramp — but a second Iran-aligned front opening against Saudi Arabia's own oil infrastructure, and fresh intelligence suggesting Iran's new leader is more nuclear-inclined than his father, both cut against reading this as more than a tactical pause; the Pentagon's own casualty-count reversal further complicates Washington's ability to sustain public and congressional support for further escalation.
global.socioeconomic: Brent's whipsaw between above $100 and the high-$80s in a single day underscores how exposed trade-dependent economies like Singapore remain to a conflict that now threatens Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export capacity as well as Hormuz, while the Pentagon casualty dispute adds a domestic US political cost — deepening distrust in an already divided Congress over the war's price — just as lawmakers weigh the administration's $95bn war-budget request.

global.headline: ISRAEL LAUNCHES WEST BANK CLAMPDOWN, ARRESTS DOZENS AFTER DEADLY SETTLER-LINKED SHOOTOUT NEAR NABLUS
summary: Israeli forces arrested nearly 50 Palestinians and raided roughly 70 homes in the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, on Saturday, a day after a shootout there killed four Palestinians and two Israelis — among the deadliest single West Bank incidents in months. Palestinian officials say the violence began when Israeli settlers raided Tal; Israel's military initially described the Israeli civilians involved as hikers but later acknowledged some were armed, saying both sides opened fire before troops intervened. The clash also triggered a raid on a Nablus hospital in which Israeli forces captured two suspects. The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned the killings of the four Palestinians as a "massacre"; Israel has not announced any action against the settlers involved.
global.geopolitical: A large-scale military clampdown and mass home raids launched in response to a settler-triggered shootout — rather than any announced action against the settlers themselves — will likely reinforce Palestinian accusations of impunity for settler violence and add further strain to an already fragile West Bank security situation while global attention remains fixed on Gaza and Iran.
global.socioeconomic: Repeated mass arrests, home raids and movement restrictions compound economic hardship for West Bank Palestinians already squeezed by years of closures and settlement expansion, deepening a humanitarian and economic toll that runs parallel to, and compounds, the adjacent Gaza crisis.

global.headline: GUYANA FERRY DEATH TOLL SURGES TO 72 AS SALVAGE CREWS RACE TO RECOVER MORE BODIES
summary: Guyana's confirmed death toll from the 19 July capsizing of the 87-year-old ferry MV Barima has risen to 72, with 76 of the roughly 179 people aboard rescued and the government warning the final toll could approach 100 — what would be the country's worst maritime disaster on record. International salvage crews, including divers from Brazil and Trinidad and Tobago, are working to raise the partially submerged vessel to help determine the cause of the sinking. Police have opened a criminal investigation and detained three people, including the rescued captain and a crew member who tested positive for marijuana; a commission of inquiry has not yet been established. The ferry, a lifeline for Guyana's isolated Essequibo region, last underwent major repairs in 2024, with further maintenance scheduled for October.
global.geopolitical: A death toll approaching 100 in a country of under a million people is a national tragedy that will test Guyana's under-resourced maritime-safety regime and pressure President Irfaan Ali's government, whose oil-boom revenues have not yet visibly modernised transport infrastructure serving the remote Essequibo interior.
global.socioeconomic: The Essequibo ferry route is a lifeline for interior communities with few road links; prolonged loss of capacity from Guyana's aging ferry fleet, combined with the reputational and compensation costs of a criminal inquiry, could squeeze an already-thin regional logistics network even as the country's oil wealth grows.

global.headline: CAR RAMS BERLIN PRIDE CROWD, KILLING ONE AND INJURING AT LEAST 14; PARADE CALLED OFF, SUSPECT AT LARGE
summary: A vehicle, described by witnesses as a white van, drove into a crowd near the route of Berlin's Pride parade (Christopher Street Day) on Saturday evening, killing at least one person and injuring at least 14, some with life-threatening injuries, before crashing into a tree in Tiergarten park. Organisers cancelled the remainder of the event, which had drawn hundreds of thousands of people to the German capital. Police said they found the suspected vehicle abandoned and are conducting an "intensive search for possible suspects"; a police spokesperson said investigators have no information yet on the perpetrator's identity or motive.
global.geopolitical: An unresolved motive at a major LGBTQ+ event in Germany's capital will draw immediate scrutiny over whether this was a targeted attack, echoing a string of vehicle-ramming incidents at European public gatherings in recent years, regardless of what the investigation ultimately finds.
global.socioeconomic: Beyond the immediate human toll, an attack on one of Europe's largest Pride events — a major draw for tourism and a symbol of the city's social openness — is likely to reignite debate over vehicle-barrier security at mass public gatherings across German and European cities.

global.headline: INDIA'S 'COCKROACH' PROTESTS END IN VICTORY AS EDUCATION MINISTER RESIGNS OVER EXAM-LEAK SCANDAL
summary: India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday, handing a decisive win to the month-long, youth-led "Cockroach" protest movement that began over alleged leaks in major entrance exams and grew into a broader outcry over unemployment and government accountability. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which organised the demonstrations, said after a fresh round of talks that all its demands had been met and formally called off the protests — which had drawn tens of thousands into the streets, triggered a violent police crackdown that injured roughly 180 people on 21 July, and included a 26-day hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk that ended 23 July after Prime Minister Narendra Modi pledged a tougher anti-paper-leak law. Pradhan announced his resignation on X without directly addressing the protesters' underlying allegations.
global.geopolitical: Forcing out a sitting Cabinet minister marks a rare, concrete win for youth-led protest politics against Modi's government, a precedent other India-based social movements — and youth movements watching from elsewhere in South Asia — are likely to draw on.
global.socioeconomic: The resignation addresses the immediate accountability demand but leaves the underlying grievances — exam-system integrity and youth unemployment — largely unresolved, meaning the economic anxieties that fuelled the movement are likely to resurface without deeper reform.

singapore.headline: PRESIDENT THARMAN LAUNCHES FIVE-YEAR SG YOUTH PLAN WITH OVER 20 INITIATIVES
summary: President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and Acting Culture, Community and Youth Minister David Neo launched the SG Youth Plan on Saturday, a five-year roadmap built from youth consultations run between November 2024 and July 2025 and covering education, careers, well-being, relationships and community involvement. Among more than 20 initiatives: 12 new free "third spaces" for youths to socialise, study or pursue hobbies by end-2026; S$500 "Curiosity Credits" for 13-to-17-year-olds from Self-Help Group families to explore arts, sports, technology, culinary or sustainability interests; transformation of an 8,700+ sq m "Somerset Belt" youth precinct by 2028; and a target of roughly 20,000 social, hobby and interest-based opportunities offered annually by 2030. David Neo said Singapore's youths are "far from" a strawberry-generation stereotype and want to find success on their own terms, citing their worries about jobs, costs and missing out.
singapore.socioeconomic: A national youth-engagement push lands alongside a record-low 0.87 total fertility rate and MOM data (also released this week) showing salary and wrongful-dismissal claims at a record high — explicit government acknowledgement that cost-of-living and job-security anxieties among the young are now significant enough to warrant a dedicated, funded five-year programme rather than incremental measures.

singapore.headline: TYPHOON NOUL DISRUPTS SINGAPORE-BOUND FLIGHTS AS HONG KONG RAISES ITS HIGHEST STORM SIGNAL THIS YEAR
summary: Singapore Airlines cancelled three flights — SQ856 (Singapore–Shenzhen, 25 July), SQ855 (Shenzhen–Singapore, 26 July) and SQ899 (Hong Kong–Singapore, 26 July) — as Typhoon Noul intensified toward the Guangdong coast. Hong Kong raised its No. 9 storm signal, its most severe warning of the year so far, cancelling more than 150 flights over the weekend; Cathay Pacific cancelled all Hong Kong International Airport arrivals and departures between 1:15am and 6pm on 26 July. More than 340,000 people have been evacuated in Guangdong province, with landfall expected between Saturday evening and Sunday morning.
singapore.socioeconomic: A third disrupted Changi-linked typhoon season this run has tracked (after Bavi in July), underscoring the recurring cost extreme regional weather now imposes on Singapore's aviation-hub connectivity during peak summer travel.

singapore.headline: WOMAN LOSES OVER S$1 MILLION TO SCAMMER WHO USED AN MP'S PHOTO TO POSE AS POLICE
summary: A woman in her 60s lost more than S$1 million of her life savings over two weeks in April to a scammer who posed as a police officer, using a Member of Parliament's photo as a WhatsApp profile picture and a Ministry of Law image as a banner to appear official. Told she had an outstanding arrest warrant and warned to tell no one, she sent the scammer a daily selfie to "prove" cooperation, made 32 separate transactions, and personally delivered jewellery and other valuables to locations the scammer specified. The scam only surfaced when she turned up at a Meet-the-People Session on 21 July seeking the MP's help to unfreeze her bank account — where he recognised his own photo had been used against her. Bishan-Toa Payoh GRC MP Cai Yinzhou shared the case publicly on 23 July.
singapore.socioeconomic: A seven-figure loss to a scam borrowing an elected official's own likeness for credibility extends a pattern this pipeline has tracked all month (the S$274,000 "digit-3" impersonation wave, the S$3b money-laundering case) of scammers exploiting official-looking identities, underlining the limits of public scam-awareness campaigns against increasingly personalised social-engineering tactics.

singapore.headline: PM WONG SAYS SEARCH FOR NEXT FINANCE MINISTER STILL 'WORK IN PROGRESS'
summary: PM Lawrence Wong, who has held the Finance portfolio alongside the premiership for just over five years, said he is "always looking to find someone who will be ready to be finance minister" but that the search remains a "work in progress," declining to give a timeline. Singapore's past two finance ministers served roughly 6.5 years on average before handover, suggesting a possible window in late 2027 or early 2028; predecessors have sometimes delegated their final Budget to a successor, making the February 2027 Budget a possible signal to watch. This week's Cabinet reshuffle added Jeffrey Siow as a second Second Minister for Finance alongside Indranee Rajah — widely read as one of the candidates now being assessed for eventual readiness.
singapore.geopolitical: Domestic, no material geopolitical dimension, though continuity of Singapore's fiscal leadership matters to how the finance ministry is read externally given ongoing tariff and inflation pressures.
singapore.socioeconomic: An orderly, telegraphed succession process for the finance portfolio — rather than an abrupt handover — supports policy continuity at a time MAS and MTI are already navigating record COE prices, a record electricity tariff and the new US forced-labour tariff.

singapore.headline: MOM: SALARY AND WRONGFUL-DISMISSAL CLAIMS HIT RECORD HIGH IN 2025 AMID RETRENCHMENT WAVE
summary: MOM and the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management's Employment Standards Report 2025, released 24 July, recorded 13,083 employment claims and appeals — up from 11,685 in 2024 — lifting the incidence rate to 3.44 per 1,000 employees from 3.12. Salary claims rose to 10,801 (2.84 per 1,000, up from 2.63), with foreign-employee claims (5.16 per 1,000) rising faster than local (1.61). Wrongful-dismissal claims rose to 2,168 from 1,720, with local claims up to 0.64 per 1,000 from 0.54 and foreign claims nearly doubling to 0.44 from 0.27. Resolution rates held up — 88% of salary claims settled at TADM, 92% of claimants fully recovered what they were owed (down from 94%), and total sums recovered rose to S$22 million from S$19 million; 67% of wrongful-dismissal claims settled at TADM, with the remaining third proceeding to the Employment Claims Tribunals. MOM attributed the rise to "increase in dismissals, retrenchments, and business closures" rather than any deterioration in employment standards.
singapore.socioeconomic: A record claims volume corroborates this pipeline's Q1 2026 retrenchment data (3,830, the highest since Q3 2023) with a fuller, full-year 2025 picture of labour-market strain, adding a further cost-of-living and job-security data point for MAS's policy calculus and reinforcing the backdrop against which today's SG Youth Plan explicitly cites youth anxiety over jobs.

word.definition: A manuscript or surface on which the original writing has been erased or scraped away to make room for new text, though traces of the earlier writing often remain visible; more broadly, something bearing visible traces of an earlier form beneath a later one.
word.etymology: From Greek palímpsēstos ("scraped again"), from pálin ("again") + psēstós ("rubbed smooth"), from psân ("to rub, scrape").
word.example: The Pentagon's casualty website became an unwitting palimpsest this week: the confirmed US death toll was quietly rubbed down from 18 to 14, but the erased names — including Sgt Angel Rampersad's — remained vivid enough in senators' and families' memories to trigger an outrage the department could not scrape away as easily as a webpage.
